1994 · 61 million pagers (Pager users worldwide)
1995 · Paging begins in India (Licensed paging operators)

How does a pager work?

Before mobiles, a beep on your belt meant someone needed you. Open a 1990s pager in 3D, type a message into a real POCSAG encoder, add radio noise and watch ten check bits repair it.

→ Before mobiles, millions carried a pager: a pocket radio that only listens.
→ Inside: a loop antenna, a receiver, a crystal, a decoder chip, a buzz motor and one AA battery.
→ You phone the paging centre, and your message joins a queue.
→ Tall towers shout it across the whole city at the same instant. Only one pager answers.
→ Each letter becomes 7 bits, packed into 32-bit codewords with 10 bits of error checking.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/pagerclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a pager work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Before mobiles, a beep on your belt meant someone needed you. Open a 1990s pager in 3D, type a message into a real POCSAG encoder, add radio noise and watch ten check bits repair it.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/pagerclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/pagerclear

In this video:
• A radio that only listens. A pager is a pocket receiver with a loop antenna, a crystal-tuned receiver, a decoder chip, a small LCD, a buzz motor and one AA battery.
• One call, a whole city. You phoned a paging centre and an operator typed your words, or the centre read your keypad tones.
• Words become codewords. In the POCSAG code each character is a 7-bit number, and bits are packed into 32-bit codewords: a flag, 20 message bits, 10 BCH check bits and a parity bit.
• Ten bits that fix mistakes. Noise flips bits on the way.
• Why pagers lasted. A pager listens only for the sync word and its own frame, so its radio is off about 80% of the time, and it never transmits.
• India's short pager boom. India auctioned paging licences for 27 cities in 1992 and services began in 1995.

Glassbox opens one box a day: an interactive model of how something works, plus the code behind it.
